years.summary: Scope: spring and autumn 2023, 18 task slots (19 rows with 8.1/8.2 split), 420 points offered. By PRIMARY module: TE1 about 110 of 420 points (26%): S2, S4, S9, A1, A3. TE2/TE3-only tasks (no TE1 content to speak of) are 150 of 420 (36%): S1, S3, S5, A2, A5, A6, A7. The remaining 160 points are mixed tasks where TE1 supplies part of the content (S6, S7, S8, A4, A8, A9). Tasks that draw on TE1 content at all (primary or mixed) are 270 of 420 (64%), which matches expected answer 1 only at its upper end: TE1 is present in about two thirds of the points offered, but is the main subject of only about a quarter. Coverage of those 270 TE1-touching points by our ten topics: full 20 (S2 exercise-facility closure), partial 230, none 20 (A1 nutrients). So our TE1 topics give a full-marks basis for about 7% of the TE1-touching points and a partial basis for 85%. Verdicts on the expected answers: (1) REFINED: TE1 appears in about 64% of points, not one third to a half, but mostly mixed with TE2/TE3; only 26% is TE1-primary. (2) PARTLY RIGHT: asked TE1 areas were nutrition (specific nutrients, bone health), exercise, sleep, mental health and emotions, the stages-of-change model, sexual health (ethics of STIs), study wellbeing and noise. Determinants of health appear as a lens (S2, S6, S7, A9) rather than as a task of their own. The four behaviour models appear only once as a direct task (A3, stages of change) and once indirectly (A5, risk perception); WRONG that they are asked most, and neither session applied TPB, SCT or the health belief model to a case. Stress and crises were not asked directly. (3) RIGHT: TE2 (research methods and reliability S5, A2, A6; health communication S3; substances inside A4/S4) and TE3 (child mortality S1, prioritisation A7, STI ethics S8, risk and disease) carry the rest; a TE1-only student cannot cover the exam. (4) RIGHT in direction, REFINED in detail: the exam is information-processing heavy (each 20 and 30 point task is split roughly half content, half 'tiedonkäsittely' by a table with concept use, application, analysis, evaluation, creation, argumentation; several tasks deduct 3-5 points if the supplied material is not used). Only 9 of 18 slots have visible material (text, map, chart, table, video); 9 have none (list/define/explain tasks), so the exam is not mostly material-based; it is recall of specific content plus structured analysis. Our K-tasks mirror the task LENGTHS (A20, B20, C30) and use fictional texts, but they lean on true/false, error-spotting and table-filling, while the real exam adds: a list of items with a count-based rubric (S3, A1, A9, S9), definitions with an example (A2), drawing a model (A3.1), real statistics and charts or maps (S6, A6) and videos. (5) PARTLY RIGHT: applying the models to material was NOT a thin spot in the topics (te1-02 K3 does it) but it was also not tested; real thin spots are specific nutrition facts (te1-04 deliberately gives none), bone, brain, noise and hearing health, emotions and physiology, the ethics-analysis frame (values, rights, consequences, duties, motives, virtues; this is TE3.s7 but TE1 sexual-health tasks need it), the Ottawa charter's five action areas, and reading statistics (te1-01 task 3 only opens the Kouluterveyskysely page; no task on survey vs register data or on a regional map). Largest content gaps in TE1 topics: (a) micronutrients and bone health (S4, A1) with neutral, linked, non-numeric treatment compatible with the site's safe-messaging rule (the exam asks facts like which nutrient aids iron absorption or the vitamin D source, which the site avoids; recommend linking to Ruokavirasto and adding a fact-sheet table without numbers or amounts, or flagging that exam-readiness needs a separate reference page); (b) alcohol, nicotine and the brain (A4; TE2); (c) emotions, hormones and health including indirect behavioural links (S9); (d) noise and the learning environment plus the Ottawa action areas (A8); (e) the ethical analysis frame and the Finnish communicable-disease classification for STIs (S8); (f) environmental crisis and mental health (S7: climate anxiety, national and community promotion measures); (g) loneliness and social media (A9, S3). Recommendations: add to TE1 topics 'exam-style' tasks of type: list-with-count (open question where the rubric counts distinct points), define-and-exemplify, draw-and-explain a model (stages of change), read a chart or map, and a material task where the answer must cite the supplied text (rubric deducts when it does not). Add a short 'tiedonkäsittely' rubric page (concept use, application, analysis, evaluation, argumentation) used by all model answers. TE2 must carry research concepts (empirical, qualitative, longitudinal, case-control), reliability of a study report, survey vs register data, health communication and social media, alcohol/nicotine and the brain; TE3 must carry child mortality and public-health history, prioritisation ethics, the ethical analysis frame, communicable diseases law and risk-factor analysis of NCDs. Caveats: only 2 sessions; the task descriptions rely on YTL's grading pages not on the papers; coverage judgments rest on keyword search plus reading the student sections of te1-01, 02, 04, 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 10, and te1-01 and te1-02 exam sections; the model answers (Mallivastaukset) in the topics were not read fully; another workflow may be editing them.

tasks.description: Put five public-health measures that cut child mortality in chronological order (child health clinics, vaccination, antibiotics, hospital network, national public health act) and explain in a written part why each reduced child mortality.
tasks.material: source 1.A (not reproduced on the grading page)
tasks.note: Public-health history, epidemiological transition and Finnish services are TE3 content; no TE1 topic touches child mortality, neuvola or vaccination history.

tasks.description: What health effects can closing sports facilities during pandemic restrictions have? Give examples and classify them (for example by individual / community / society, or physical / mental / social).
tasks.material: text: a news article about corona restrictions on sports facilities (not reproduced on the page)
tasks.note: te1-05 (benefits of moving, rest, recovery, four levels of influence) with te1-01 (levels, mechanism chains) gives the skill and most content. Minor gaps: infection-spread trade-off, population-level and economic effects, injury or sport-switching examples; te1-01 K3 and te1-05 K3 train the same classify-and-explain move.

tasks.description: List the possibilities and the harms of social media in health promotion; no essay needed, one point per correct item and at most 10 p for one-sided answers.
tasks.note: Health communication and its reliability are TE2.s2. te1-03 (terveystiedon lukutaito) and te1-04 (ruokapuhe) give only a faint base; no TE1 page treats social media, influencers, misinformation or peer support online.

tasks.description: Analyse how a fictional woman's food choices and lifestyle affect her bone health (calcium, vitamin D, BMI, alcohol, smoking, exercise, heredity).
tasks.note: te1-04 and te1-05 give the frame (nutrition, movement, determinants) but contain no calcium, vitamin D, bone health or osteoporosis content, and by design no amounts; alcohol and smoking are TE2.s8 and are not in any TE1 page. A student would have to bring the facts from elsewhere.

tasks.description: Which details should be added to a news article on a slipping-accident study so that its reliability could be judged (reliability and validity, researcher and funders, sample, response rate, peer review)?
tasks.material: text 5.A (a news report of a study)
tasks.note: Research process and reliability are TE2.s1. te1-03 task 2 (compare two sources) is the only nearby practice; no TE1 page names sample, reliability or validity.

tasks.description: Discuss reasons for regional differences in coronary heart disease prevalence in Finland (lifestyle, heredity, socioeconomic factors; age is not accepted since the data are age-standardised).
tasks.note: te1-01 gives determinants on four levels, mechanism chains and health differences, which is the right frame. Lacks: disease-specific risk factors and heritability, reading a map of age-standardised prevalence, non-communicable disease content (TE3), and any statistical-literacy task.

tasks.description: Discuss health-promotion measures that can support mental health during environmental crises (effects such as climate anxiety; national policy, communities, everyday choices, education, health care).
tasks.material: text 7.A (an appeal by mental-health organisations about the environment)
tasks.note: te1-08 covers protective factors at individual, community and society level and te1-01 lists global factors including climate, so the structure is there. Lacks: environmental crisis and climate anxiety, sustainable-development link (TE2.s4), national-level promotion instruments (legislation, funding, monitoring), health-communication and service measures, and a material-based task on this theme.

tasks.description: Discuss ethical questions of falling ill with a sexually transmitted disease using a first-person account (communicable-disease law classes, notification, shame, values, rights, duties, virtues).
tasks.material: text 8.A (a personal account of an STI, shame and telling partners)
tasks.note: te1-06 covers STIs, symptomless infection and stigma; te1-07 covers rights and an ethical-question frame; te1-03 K3 trains ethical analysis. Lacks: the named ethical perspectives (values, norms, duties, motives, consequences, rights, virtues, TE3.s7), the legal classification of communicable diseases, duty to inform partners and criminal responsibility, and use of a text about a person's experience as material.

tasks.description: Examine the links between emotions and health and the factors that influence them (physiological and hormonal links, indirect links through behaviour, sleep and care seeking, emotion skills).
tasks.task_type: open concept essay (count rubric with direct, indirect and influencing factors)
tasks.note: te1-09 explains the stress reaction, load and coping, te1-08 protective factors and te1-01 emotion regulation as a resource. Lacks: hormones and the nervous system, indirect pathways (emotional eating, substances, symptom perception, treatment adherence), emotion skills and suppression, culture and temperament as influencing factors. A concept-essay task with no material is not among our K tasks.

tasks.description: Twenty true-or-false statements about vitamin C, vitamin D, calcium, iron and iodine, one point each.
tasks.note: te1-04 names vitamins and minerals only in general and deliberately gives no specific nutrient facts or amounts. None of the five nutrients is mentioned in any TE1 topic. If the site wants exam readiness here it needs a linked fact table (sources, functions, absorption) without amounts, or an explicit pointer to Ruokavirasto pages.

tasks.description: Define four research types (empirical, qualitative, longitudinal, case-control) and give a health-research example for each; 900-character limit.
tasks.note: Research methods are TE2.s1 and TE2.t1. No TE1 topic covers study designs; te1-02 K3 only touches survey data lightly.

tasks.description: Draw a diagram of the stages of change model including relapse (3.1, 5 p) and fill a table naming and explaining each stage (3.2, 15 p).
tasks.task_type: draw a model and explain it
tasks.note: te1-02 lists the five stages in order with a one-line gloss, mentions relapse and says what support fits each stage. Lacks explanation depth the rubric rewards (pros and cons in contemplation, self-efficacy and social support in preparation, relapse as learning, monitoring in maintenance) and any draw-the-model or fill-the-table task: our tasks use the model in a case, not as a diagram.

tasks.description: Judge five claims about brain health (sleep, a night without sleep, all exercise, alcohol, nicotine) as true, false or both, with a justification for each.
tasks.note: te1-05 covers sleep and exercise benefits for concentration, memory and mood. Lacks: concussion risk in contact sports, effects of sleep deprivation on safety, and alcohol and nicotine effects on the brain and the fetus (TE2.s8, in no TE1 page). The claim-evaluation format also needs more practice than our true-or-false tasks give.

tasks.description: Analyse the concept of health risk from three texts (epidemiological relative risk, environmental exposure risk, subjective everyday risk); a deduction applies if texts are not used.
tasks.note: Risk as a concept belongs to TE2 (reasoning biases, risk communication) and TE3 (risk factors). te1-02 (health belief model, perceived susceptibility) touches only the subjective dimension. No TE1 page defines relative risk, exposure, dose or the subjective versus objective distinction.

tasks.description: Analyse why survey data (FinTerveys 2017) and hospital register data differ on obesity, high blood pressure and depression; reliability of both sources.
tasks.task_type: analysis of a chart (source and data criticism)
tasks.note: Mostly TE2 (research reliability, data sources). te1-01 task 3 sends the student to the Kouluterveyskysely page, which is the only data-source practice in TE1; no task compares a survey with a register, or names non-response, self-report or coverage.

tasks.description: Analyse ethical aspects of prioritisation in health care (what it is, why it is needed, levels, values, rights, consequences, motives, duties).
tasks.note: Prioritisation and the health-care ethical principles are TE3.s9 and TE3.s7.

tasks.description: Explain how noise affects study ability (personal resources, study skills, teaching and guidance, learning environment), with examples.
tasks.note: te1-10 defines study ability, demands versus resources and the study environment, which is the right frame. Lacks: noise and hearing health, the physiological and cognitive effects of noise, and the four-part study-ability model used in the rubric.
tasks.part_label: Part 3 (30 p, sub-task of a 30 p task)

tasks.description: Propose ways of reducing noise exposure in a learning environment using the five action areas of the WHO health-promotion model.
tasks.task_type: apply a model to propose measures
tasks.material: table of the WHO health-promotion areas with examples
tasks.note: te1-01 defines health promotion, its actors and how to make a reasoned proposal (te1-01 task 3 and K3 train this). Lacks: the Ottawa action areas (policy, supportive environments, community action, personal skills, services), noise and the physical environment (TE2.s3), and a task with a supplied model table.
tasks.part_label: Part 3 (30 p, sub-task of a 30 p task)

tasks.description: How does social media affect young people's loneliness? Positive and negative effects, with the text and video as material; deductions if the material is not used.
tasks.task_type: analysis with positive and negative effects
tasks.note: te1-08 covers belonging, protective community factors and stigma; te1-07 mentions loneliness and belonging. Lacks: loneliness as a concept, social media (comparison, filter bubbles, cyberbullying, addictive use, peer groups), and a task on video or multi-source material.

years.summary:
Coverage of the 2024 exam by TE1: the YTL exam has 9 tasks per session worth 210 points in all, and the student answers 5 of them (120 points). Counting all 210 points per session, tasks drawn mainly from TE1 are worth about 40 points in spring 2024 (19%) and about 105 in autumn 2024 (50%). Adding mixed tasks where TE1 is a main strand brings those to about 100 (48%) in spring and 155 (74%) in autumn, which is an upper bound.

Spring 2024 TE1-primary tasks: sexual rights (T5) and medicalization (T6). TE1-led mixed tasks: mushroom-picking health effects (T7), the obesity task with WHO action areas (T9.2), and a few TE1 statements in T1. TE2 and TE3 carry the rest: flu versus cold, disease explanation models, radon, biobank ethics, infectious and non-communicable disease statements.
Autumn 2024 TE1-primary tasks: statements 2.1-2.3 (health literacy, sitting, traumatic crisis), determinants of health in a four-level model (T4), hypnogram (T5), eustress versus distress (T6), food labels (T7). Mixed: tooth brushing by sex, age and education (T1), clean water (T9). TE2 and TE3: mixed-methods statement 2.4, infectious diseases table (T3), addiction (T8).

How well our TE1 topics cover them:
- Full: medicalization (te1-03), sitting (te1-05), traumatic crisis (te1-09), determinants of health on several levels (te1-01), with one note that the exam's four-level model (individual, lifestyle, environments, society) differs from our individual, community, society, global split, so students must be taught to map between the two.
- Partial: sexual rights in an institution (te1-07), health-literacy and prevention versus promotion statement (te1-03), mushroom health dimensions (te1-01/05/08), eustress and distress (te1-09, no term or structured multi-perspective comparison), sleep significance (te1-05), food labels (te1-04), obesity measures (te1-04/01), tooth brushing table (te1-01), water (te1-04).
- None: sleep stages and hypnogram reading (12 of 20 points in autumn T5), line-chart drawing from a table (spring T9.1), WHO/Ottawa five action areas, nutrition label reading including the Heart Symbol, oral health, health-inequality reading of FinTerveys tables.

Expected-answer check:
(1) 'TE1 appears in a third to a half of tasks' is roughly right but refined: about one fifth of the points in spring and about half in autumn when strictly TE1, with mixed tasks raising these to around half and three quarters.
(2) Areas asked most: right for determinants, sleep, stress and crisis, nutrition, sexual rights; refined because mental health appears only through crisis and resilience; wrong for the four behaviour models, which no task in either 2024 session asked.
(3) TE2/TE3 make up the rest: right (research methods, infection, radon, addiction, biobank ethics, disease models, health inequality); a TE1-only student could not cover the exam, and could hardly fill the TE1 share given the gaps above.
(4) Exam weights information processing: right; most tasks use material (tables, a figure, a graph, labels, text, video) and scoring splits content and information handling in 10+10 or 15+15 for 20- and 30-point tasks, with material references required (5 points deducted otherwise). Our TE1 exam tasks follow the 20/20/30 shape and are material-based on paper, but the sampled topics show concept recall and short statements dominate and few tasks need drawing a chart or reading real statistics tables.
(5) Thin spots: statistics reading right; applying models to material not tested in 2024 (wrong for this year); phenomena with current examples partly right (medicalization appears with materials); new thin spots not predicted: sleep stages, nutrient-level label assessment, WHO action areas, drawing a graph, writing a table as a screenshot answer.
Recommendations hinted by the data: add to te1-05 a sleep-stage section with a hypnogram task; add to te1-04 a nutrition-label task; add to te1-01 a determinants task using the exam's four-level model wording and a table-reading task by sex, age and education; add to te1-01 or te1-03 the WHO health promotion action areas applied to a weight or other health issue; add to te1-09 an eustress and distress comparison; add a graph-drawing task; TE3 must carry disease explanation models, biobank ethics, infectious disease, and TE2 addiction, radon and research methods.

tasks.description: Twenty true-or-false statements, 1 p each: health literacy and activity guidelines, placebo and research design, tobacco, e-cigarettes, cannabis and COPD, blood pressure, cholesterol, heart disease and diabetes, cancer prevention and vaccines.
tasks.note: Only a few statements are TE1 (health literacy, physical activity guidelines). Most draw on TE2 and TE3. te1-03/te1-05 cover only those few; no TE1 topic treats blood pressure, cholesterol or vaccines.

tasks.description: Compare common cold and influenza on five perspectives (definition and cause, prevalence, symptoms, treatment, prevention) in a table the student builds and attaches as a screenshot.
tasks.note: Infectious disease content belongs to TE3; te1-01 mentions infections only in passing.

tasks.description: Put four historical models of disease explanation (demonic, humoral, miasma, multi-causal) in order and describe each one's view of causes and treatment, in a table.
tasks.note: Disease explanation models are TE3.s1; no TE1 topic covers them.

tasks.description: Describe radon as the environmental risk shown on a map, its health effects (lung cancer) and factors that change the size of the risk (soil, building, ventilation, exposure time, smoking).
tasks.note: Physical environment and health belongs to TE2; te1-01 treats environment only as a general determinant.

tasks.description: Explain with examples how a school or other educational institution can support students' sexual rights, naming the rights and concrete actions.
tasks.note: te1-07 covers rights, consent, diversity and a school-level proposal, but it does not appear to list the full set of rights (privacy, protection, participation) or institution-level measures (equality plan, anonymous surveys, student health services, parents and internship cooperation); partly covered by te1-06.

tasks.description: Identify the phenomenon in the materials as medicalization, describe it and discuss positive and negative effects for society and healthcare and for the individual.
tasks.note: te1-03 defines medicalization with benefits and harms; it lacks the terms overdiagnosis, overtesting and overtreatment and the explicit society versus individual structure, and does not practise identifying the phenomenon from a material.

tasks.description: Analyse health effects of mushroom picking on physical, mental and social health, positive and negative, using the materials.
tasks.task_type: analysis of an activity's health effects from material
tasks.note: te1-01, te1-05 and te1-08 give the dimensions and mechanism chains, but there is no task applying dimensions to a nature activity with risks (poisoning, ticks, injury), and no nature-environment link (TE2.s3).

tasks.description: Analyse biobank activity from an ethical perspective (values, virtues, consequences, rights, duties, motives, norms) from several actors' viewpoints, using a video.
tasks.note: Ethical analysis frameworks are TE3.s7; te1-03, te1-07 and te1-09 practise a simpler ethical analysis that is partial preparation only.

tasks.description: Draw a line chart of obesity by age group over years from a table and briefly explain main results (sex, time, age differences).
tasks.task_type: data processing: chart drawing and interpretation
tasks.note: No TE1 topic has the student draw a chart or interpret a time series by group; te1-04 deliberately avoids weight figures.

tasks.description: Describe societal measures to promote weight management and reduce obesity, organised by the WHO's five health promotion action areas.
tasks.task_type: explanation of societal measures with framework
tasks.note: te1-04 task 5 asks school or society proposals and te1-01 covers health promotion, but the five action areas (policy, supportive environments, community action, personal skills, services) are absent, as are taxes, marketing limits and early intervention at service level.

tasks.description: Explain the main results on tooth brushing twice a day by sex, age, education and region from a survey table.
tasks.note: te1-01 covers determinants such as education and a data-reading task on youth wellbeing, but not reading differences by group in a population table, or oral health habits.

tasks.description: Pick the best option about health literacy, medicalization and prevention versus health promotion, and justify why the others are wrong.
tasks.note: te1-03 covers health literacy as source evaluation and medicalization; the five-part definition of health literacy and the prevention versus health promotion distinction are not clearly taught.

tasks.description: Judge a statement on sitting and a lukio student's health, explaining that breaking up sitting helps and standing still is not strength training.
tasks.note: te1-05 teaches breaking up long sitting; strength training recommendations are linked, not copied.

tasks.description: Pick the best option on an acute traumatic crisis, defining it and linking it to coping ability, sense of coherence and resilience.
tasks.note: te1-09 separates developmental and traumatic crisis; sense of coherence and resilience appear in te1-08 only, a short link would close it.

tasks.description: Pick the best option on mixed methods in health research, separating it from data sources and sampling.
tasks.note: Research methods are TE2.

tasks.description: Build a table with transmission route for five infectious diseases (Lyme, HIV, influenza, malaria, salmonella) and two prevention methods each, from given lists.
tasks.material: blank table template and two lists
tasks.note: TE3 content; te1-06 touches sexually transmitted infections and HIV only in passing.

tasks.description: Using a four-level model of health prerequisites, give four examples per level with a justification (individual, lifestyle, environments, societal conditions), 5 p each.
tasks.material: figure of a four-level model with examples
tasks.note: te1-01 covers determinants and mechanism chains. The exam's levels differ from our individual, community, society, global split, so students need to practise mapping to the exam's model wording.

tasks.description: Name and describe sleep stages A to D shown on a hypnogram (awake, light, deep, REM).
tasks.note: te1-05 has no sleep stages, no NREM and REM descriptions and no hypnogram.

tasks.description: Explain the health significance of deep sleep and REM sleep (recovery, immunity, growth hormone, memory, emotions).
tasks.note: te1-05 gives general benefits of sleep (recovery, memory, emotion) but not by stage, immune function or growth hormone.

tasks.description: Compare eustress and distress: define both and compare on causes, physiological reaction, manifestations, consequences and coping.
tasks.note: te1-09 separates helpful short-term stress from overload, but lacks the terms eustress and distress and a multi-perspective comparison (physiology, manifestations, consequences, coping).

tasks.description: Assess the healthiness of four foods (yogurt, cheese, rye bread, spread) from product information and nutrition labels against Finnish recommendations; explain labels and the Heart Symbol.
tasks.note: te1-04 links to recommendations and lists nutrients but gives no label reading, no fat quality, salt, fibre, sugar or calcium assessment, and no Heart Symbol.

tasks.description: Analyse the mechanisms (biological, psychological, social), key features and health harms of addiction, substance versus behavioural, using the materials.
tasks.note: Addiction is TE2.

tasks.description: Justify why water and its purity matter for health: fluid balance, contaminated water risks, hygiene, and societal effects of shortage.
tasks.note: te1-04 names water as a nutrient; fluid balance and everything on contamination, hygiene and global shortage is TE2 or TE3.

tasks.description: Write the single health-education concept that matches each of 20 definitions (sexual and gender minorities, contraception, diseases, substances, society and environment).
tasks.task_type: concept recall (short answer, one point each)
tasks.note: te1-06 and te1-07 cover the sexuality and diversity concepts and contraception. Substance, disease and environment concepts are TE2/TE3. Our concept tasks are true/false, not 20 definitions to name.

tasks.description: List the health effects of a holiday trip and sort them into physical, psychological and social health.
tasks.task_type: open listing and classification (2 p per correctly classed effect)
tasks.note: te1-01 teaches health as a multi-dimensional whole and its background factors. Infection risk and accidents while travelling are only incidental.

tasks.description: Explain how a person can strengthen the body's resistance to illness (lifestyle, hygiene, vaccines, antibiotics, age).
tasks.task_type: open explanation (2 p per means, 3 p when explained)
tasks.note: te1-04, te1-05 and te1-09 cover the lifestyle means (food, exercise, sleep, stress). Vaccination, hygiene, antibiotics and the idea of resistance itself are absent from TE1 (no hits for vaccines or resistance).

tasks.description: Argue why using home tests (tick-borne disease, covid, flu) takes health competence, using two pictures of test kits.
tasks.material: two images (test kits); health competence has five areas (knowledge, skills, critical thinking, self-knowledge, ethical responsibility)
tasks.note: Health competence (terveysosaaminen) with its five areas is not named in any TE1 topic. te1-03 (comparing sources, medicalisation) and te1-02 (self-management programme) are only adjacent. Self-testing and self-care are TE3.s6, source evaluation is TE2.

tasks.description: Discuss why health differences between population groups in Finland should be narrowed.
tasks.note: te1-01 gives background factors and mentions health inequality. The arguments the exam wants (cost, services, employment, ethics, social peace, international commitments) and groups by language and migration are TE3.s10 depth. Our topics lack a justify-the-case task.

tasks.description: Justify with examples what emotional skills a social media user needs (recognising, regulating and expressing emotions; comparison, fear of missing out, algorithms).
tasks.note: te1-08 and te1-09 cover mental-health protective factors and coping, but no topic mentions social media or emotional skills. The social-media environment belongs to TE2.s3 (psychosocial environment).

tasks.description: Draw bar charts of women's and men's weekly alcohol use 1968-2023 from two tables, attach them and state the main findings.

tasks.task_type: applied analysis with a given framework
tasks.material: table of WHO action areas in the task

tasks.description: Name and describe two health phenomena of a person in a given text (orthorexia and anorexia).
tasks.note: te1-04 mentions eating disorders, but orthorexia is absent, and no topic describes eating disorders as phenomena with their features. Per the safe-messaging rule our pages may describe them only at a general level and with help links, which limits full coverage by design.

tasks.description: Analyse the factors that predispose a person to these two phenomena at individual, community, society and global level, using the text.
tasks.task_type: analytical explanation (content 0-10, information handling 0-10; 5 points off if the material is not used)
tasks.note: The method matches te1-01 (factors at four levels, mechanism chains) and te1-08. Missing: applying it to a given case text with a penalty for leaving the material out, and the eating-disorder content itself.

tasks.description: Analyse ethical challenges of AI-produced text, based on a 14-year-old's question about energy drinks and the AI's answer.
tasks.task_type: ethical analysis (content 0-15, information handling 0-15; 5 points off if the material is not used)
tasks.note: TE3.s7 ethical viewpoints (values, norms, duties, rights, consequences, virtues) and critical reading are not TE1. Only the energy-drink nutrition link touches te1-04.

tasks.description: Choose the right option for each of ten statements (depression, health belief model, WHO, stroke, tuberculosis, rheumatic disease, 1972 public health act, metabolic syndrome, retrospective study, carcinogens).
tasks.note: Only two of ten items are TE1 (depression, te1-08, and health belief model, te1-02). The rest are disease, history and method items from TE2 and TE3. Our true/false tasks do not use the scoring with a penalty.

tasks.note: te1-02 teaches self-management programmes (omahoito) as applied behaviour models, but the term self-care (itsehoito) and the societal benefits, harms, medication use and health literacy come from TE3.s6.

tasks.description: Define lactose-free, milk-free, gluten-free and vegan diets, say who needs each and describe the health aspects, including nutrient adequacy.
tasks.task_type: short written explanations in four parts
tasks.note: te1-04 covers general nutrition and official recommendations, but it has no special diets (no lactose, gluten, vegan content), no food allergy or coeliac disease, and no key nutrients of vegan eating.

tasks.description: Define cognitive biases, explain how they affect health decisions and apply them to three people described in a text.
tasks.note: Thinking biases are TE2.s1. TE1 has the 'attitudes and beliefs' side only through the models in te1-02.

tasks.description: Assess, using an advertisement text, how reliable health communication can be told from unreliable.
tasks.note: te1-03 compares sources and covers alternative treatments (TE1.s3) and te1-04 evaluates food claims. Missing are the marketing tactics (testimonials, fear, appeal to nature, conspiracy claims) and the evidence-based versus belief-based distinction as a criterion list.

tasks.description: Analyse how ecological, economic, social and cultural sustainability affect health and well-being.
tasks.note: Sustainable development and health is TE2.s4. No TE1 topic treats it.

tasks.description: Name the model in a diagram with three curves, then analyse how mortality, births and population change across its five stages and why (sub-parts 2, 3 and 25 points).
tasks.note: The epidemiological transition is TE3.s4. Nothing in TE1.

tasks.description: Analyse the ethics of abortion from a global view using several ethical viewpoints, with an introductory text of WHO figures and legal background.
tasks.material: short introductory text in the task (WHO figures, law)
tasks.note: Ethical and legal questions are TE3.s8. te1-07 (sexual rights) is adjacent and gives only the rights perspective, with no ethical analysis frame. Abortion law and unsafe abortion are not in our TE1 topics.

tasks.description: Assess a 17-year-old's movement, eating, sleep and substance use against the national recommendations and show how these habits connect.
tasks.task_type: analysis of a data table against recommendations
tasks.note: te1-05 (movement, rest, sleep with official recommendations; K3 is a material analysis) and te1-04 (meals) match well. Missing: tobacco, nicotine and alcohol for minors (no hits in TE1), and linking the habits to each other in one answer.

years.summary: Two sessions read (spring 2025, autumn 2025), 20 task rows, with sub-parts 7 and 8 in spring split. Of the 210 points offered each session (three tasks of 20 in Part 1, three of 20 in Part 2, three of 30 in Part 3), about 50 points (24 percent) sit in tasks that are mainly TE1: spring 2, 8.1 and 8.2 (50 points); autumn 3 and 9 (50 points). Spring task 3 is TE1 with TE3 (20 more). Everything else is TE2 or TE3, or mixed. Our TE1 topics cover well only spring task 2. No task is covered 'full' beyond that. The topics cover partly the TE1 parts of 8.2, 3, autumn 3 and 9, and the framework or recall parts of several mixed tasks. Against the expected answer: (1) right that the exam draws on all modules, and the TE1 share is lower than the 'third to half' guess, close to a quarter of the points offered. (2) Refined: asked TE1 areas were health dimensions, eating disorders and their predisposing factors, nutrition (special diets), movement/sleep/substance use against recommendations. Not asked in these two sessions: stress, sexuality (except concepts), study well-being, and the four behaviour models beyond one multiple-choice item. (3) Right: TE2 and TE3 carry most of the exam (sources, communication, bias, sustainability, ethics, transition, inequality, self-care). (4) Right: seven of the 20 task rows use material (tables, texts, diagrams, images) and graph building (7.1) and framework application (7.2) are missing from TE1. Our K1/K2/K3 types (true/false, comparison, material analysis) do not include multiple choice with a penalty, concept naming, listing and classifying, or table-to-chart. (5) Thin spots confirmed: applying to a case text with the material-use rule; health inequality justifications; reading tables against recommendations (te1-05 fine). Kouluterveyskysely not seen in these exams. Gaps to add to TE1: substances (alcohol, tobacco, nicotine) in te1-05 or a new topic or link to TE2, special diets and food allergy in te1-04, eating-disorder features (safe messaging), WHO five action areas in te1-01, immune resistance and vaccines in te1-05, health competence (terveysosaaminen), emotional skills and social media in te1-08. Caveat: only two sessions read; four-year view and 2023, 2024, 2026 belong to other readers. Task descriptions rest on page summaries from WebFetch; the exam papers themselves were not opened.

years.summary:
Both 2026 sessions were mapped from the exam pages at the Yle Abitreenit mirror (spring 20.3.2026, autumn 16.9.2026). Both have 9 tasks and 120 points; a candidate answers 5. Coverage of TE1 is partial. The spring hyvän vastauksen piirteet PDF could not be read and the autumn one was not found, so mapping rests on task wording and material titles. Our topics were checked by headings and keywords only.

Points offered by module (all tasks, not what a candidate answers). Spring: TE1 only for tasks 3 (20), 4 (20), 6 (20) = 60 of 180 offered; mixed with TE1 share 1, 2, 5, 8 = 90; TE3 only 7 (30); TE2 only 9 (30). Autumn: pure TE1 only task 5 (20); partial TE1 in 6 (20) and 9 (30); the other six tasks (1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8 = 140 p) are TE2 or TE3. A candidate who chooses wisely can answer mostly TE1 in spring (tasks 3, 4, 6, plus the TE1 parts of 1, 8) but not in autumn, where TE1 is at most tasks 5, 6 and 9.

Versus the expected answer: (1) 'TE1 appears in a third to half of tasks' is roughly right for spring (about 6 of 9 tasks touch TE1) and refined for autumn (3 of 9). (2) Most-asked TE1 areas: theory models (both sessions, full match), health definition/determinants, nutrition, sexual health. Sleep, exercise, mental health, stress and study wellbeing were not asked in either 2026 session, so the expectation is wrong for those. (3) Right: TE1 alone cannot cover the exam, especially autumn. (4) Right and sharpened: material-based tasks with figures, tables, charts, video and study designs dominate; autumn task 1 and 9 rely on data interpretation. (5) Partly right: model application is well covered by te1-02; gaps are the WHO definition critique, fertility, fat quality/food triangle, ethics in food choices, and figure-based inequality analysis; Kouluterveyskysely is not what the exam used.

Exam-task type match: our K1/K2/K3 types (error spotting, table completion, material analysis, theory application, ethical analysis) match real types (error spotting, table building, cloze, theory application, ethics). Missing in ours: research-plan drafting, multiple choice with penalty marking, drop-down cloze, video material and image-reading tasks. Our K3 at 30 points is used for theory and data analysis, while real 20-point tasks are the model-application ones.

critic.module_shares:
Scope: 8 sessions (spring and autumn 2023-2026), 72 tasks, 1680 points offered (210 per session; a candidate answers 5 tasks for 120). I used the readers' module labels with four critic corrections: A23-5 (risk concept) and A26-7 (work ability) are TE2, not mixed; A23-8.1 (noise and study ability) is TE1 (TE1.s7); A26-9 (cancer costs by WHO action areas) is mixed, not TE3. One reader error: the 2026 reader wrote "60 of 180 offered" for spring 2026. The right figure is 60 of 210.

POINTS by module: TE1-primary 463 p (28%). Mixed with a TE1 strand 522 p (31%). TE2-only 345 p (21%). TE3-only 350 p (21%). TE1 is present in 985 p (59%) but is the main subject of only 28%.
TASKS by module (sub-parts merged; a task with sub-parts from different modules counts as mixed): TE1 20 of 72 (28%), mixed 23 (32%), TE2 15 (21%), TE3 14 (19%).
The TE1-primary share swings widely between sessions: S23 70 p, A23 48, S24 40, A24 105, S25 50, A25 50, S26 60, A26 40 (19% to 50% of 210).

Coverage of the TE1-touching points by our ten topics (1045 p, leaving out 100 p of TE2/TE3 tasks with only a marginal TE1 code): full 135 p (13%), partial 848 p (81%), none 62 p (6%). The full matches are S23-2, S24-6, A24-2.2, A24-2.3, A24-4, S25-2, S26-3.1, S26-4 and A26-5. The nones are A23-1 (nutrient facts), S24-9.1 (drawing a chart), A24-5.1 (hypnogram) and S26-6 (fertility).

Material-based: 46 of 72 tasks (64%) and 1082 p (64%) carry material. Only about 18 tasks carry real data or media (chart, map, statistics table, hypnogram, product labels, image, video). The rest carry text.
critic.te1_code_frequency: Counted over the 81 task rows, sub-parts as separate rows (rows / points touched): TE1.s4 nutrition, exercise, rest, sleep, weight 26 / 535. TE1.s1 determinants and their mechanisms, incl. health promotion 21 / 417. TE1.t1 15 / 305. TE1.s6 mental-health protective factors, stress 14 / 283. TE1.t3 9 / 202. TE1.s5 sexuality, sexual health and rights 5 / 120. TE1.s2 behaviour models 5 / 100 (A23-3 stages of change drawn as a diagram, S26-4 social cognitive theory, A26-5 planned behaviour, one A25-1 multiple-choice item on the health belief model, A23-5 marginal). TE1.s3 health-culture phenomena 5 / 85. TE1.t2 4 / 80. TE1.s7 study wellbeing 1 / 8 (A23-8.1 only). In short: s4 and s1 dominate, s6 is mid-weight, s2, s3 and s5 are occasional, and s7 is nearly absent.

versus_expected.item: 1. Exam draws on all modules; TE1 in a third to a half of tasks, often combined
versus_expected.note: All three modules are present (right). TE1 is the main subject of 28% of tasks and 28% of points. It appears at all, primary or mixed, in 60% of tasks and 59% of points. The TE1-primary share swings from 19% (S24, A26) to 50% (A24) between sessions.

versus_expected.item: 2. Most-asked TE1 areas: determinants, mental health and stress, sleep, exercise, nutrition, sexual health, the four models applied to a case
versus_expected.note: Right for nutrition (TE1.s4 is the most frequent code, 26 rows), determinants and health promotion (s1, 21 rows) and sleep. Mental health and stress are mid-weight (s6, 14 rows). Exercise and sexual health are occasional (s5, 5 rows). Wrong that the models rank among the most asked: TE1.s2 has 5 rows, and only two tasks apply a model to material (both in 2026, both fully covered by te1-02). Study wellbeing appears once. Not foreseen: the WHO action areas (4 sessions) and specific nutrient facts.

versus_expected.item: 3. TE2 and TE3 carry the rest; TE1 alone cannot cover the exam
versus_expected.note: TE2-only and TE3-only tasks are 42% of points, and mixed tasks need TE2 or TE3 content (substances, ethics frame, epidemiology). Even TE1-primary tasks such as S23-4 and A25-9 require alcohol and tobacco content that TE1 lacks. A26 offered only two TE1-primary tasks.

versus_expected.item: 4. Exam weights information processing; TE1 exam tasks lean on concept recall and lack material-based data tasks
versus_expected.note: Information processing: right (half of each 20 p and 30 p task is tiedonkäsittely, with deductions for unused material). But our tasks do not lean on recall: nearly all are material-based, on fictional text. The gap is data and media (charts, maps, tables, hypnogram, labels, video), drawing tasks and supplied frameworks. The exam also has more fact-recall formats (true/false on nutrients, concept naming, multiple choice with penalty) than our topics can support, because they omit specific facts.

versus_expected.item: 5. Thin spots: models applied to material, health-culture phenomena with current examples, reading statistics such as Kouluterveyskysely
versus_expected.note: Models applied to material: wrong, te1-02 K3 covers it and the 2026 tasks match fully. Health-culture phenomena: mostly covered (medicalisation, S24-6, full). Reading statistics: right, but the exam uses FinTerveys and population tables, charts and maps, never Kouluterveyskysely, and it also asks students to draw charts. Bigger unforeseen thin spots: the WHO action areas, nutrient facts and labels, sleep stages, the WHO definition critique, fertility, eustress and distress, social media and emotions.

Across the set, add exam formats we lack: list-and-classify with a count rubric, define-and-exemplify, multiple choice with penalty, concept naming, draw a model or chart, read a chart, map or image, apply a supplied framework, and critique a concept.
